A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AgentScore work despite the changed title. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–G are readable and support reliable matching.

before.justification: v1 reports original clinical prediction experiments, external validation, ablations, and a study with 18 clinicians in Section 5 and Appendix E.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds rule-pool comparisons, a membership-inference audit, and missing-measurement experiments.

M1.justification: The reported procedure changes missing-input handling to permit imputation before a rule defaults to false (Appendices B/D.1), and Appendix F changes final threshold fitting from Dval to Dcon. The rule grammar, agent roles, checklist structure, and prompts remain unchanged. These are limited procedural revisions, with implementation certainty limited by inconsistent split descriptions.

E1.justification: The clinical datasets, populations, and tasks in Tables 8–9 remain unchanged. v2 adds partial-observability scenarios on the existing CF and ICU mortality tasks and membership-inference evaluation using the eight MIMIC/eICU tasks. Table 1's changed mortality-horizon caption does not establish a new task; both versions' Table 8 already specifies three-year CF-UK mortality.

E2.justification: v2 adds Optimal Checklists to the main benchmark and external missingness comparisons. Table 11 adds Optimal Checklists with raw features plus generated rules, and FasterRisk, MIP, and greedy selection using AgentScore's validated rule pool. All existing PLR comparators remain; four move from the main table to the appendix.

E3.justification: New designs include shared-rule-pool controls, an oracle-based privacy audit with an identity-grouped 80/20 attacker split, and 10%/25% test-time feature dropout. Reported existing settings also change: median-imputation coverage, rule-screening/threshold-fitting splits, and Table 10's Jaccard threshold and minimum gain from 0.9/0.01 to 0.95/0.001. Conflicting prose remains, so these revisions do not establish which configurations produced the retained results or whether experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix E.2 adds controls addressing whether gains arise from rule construction or downstream assembly. E.6 adds transcript/final-checklist privacy attacks, and E.7 tests robustness to missing measurements. Existing component ablations, backbone sensitivity, risk monotonicity, checklist-size analysis, and clinician evaluation are retained.

E5.justification: Section 5.4 newly reports Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests and Cohen's d for existing ablations. Appendix D.1 changes 'one-sided' to 'two-sided', although its directional alternative remains inconsistent. Existing five-fold/five-seed reporting and baseline confidence-interval procedures are retained; additional result rows do not establish increased runs.

E6.justification: Existing Table 3 entries and Figure 3 results are retained. Added results include Optimal Checklists' mean AUROC of 0.62 versus AgentScore's 0.71, rule-pool FasterRisk/MIP/greedy means of 0.69/0.65/0.53, privacy-attack outcomes, and missingness results favoring AgentScore on CF but Optimal Checklists on ICU mortality. Table 14's full-data scores differ from Figure 3; they are newly reported results, not demonstrated same-setting performance changes.

T1.justification: The mathematical rule families, score definitions, constrained objectives, Jaccard definition, and complexity arguments in Section 2 and Appendices E.1/F remain substantively unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or mathematical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The conceptual contribution is reframed around joint derived-rule construction and checklist selection, acknowledging existing checklist learners. The abstract's central claims remain stable. The conclusion emphasizes candidate scores for prospective validation and removes the suggested extension to aviation and lending.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the shared-rule-pool results as evidence that assembly matters beyond feature construction, adds explicit privacy threat-model boundaries, and discusses task-dependent missingness behavior. It softens the expectation of monotonic improvement with advancing LLMs. However, E.7's general degradation statement conflicts with the increasing CF Optimal Checklists means in Table 14.

D1.justification: v1 promises code upon acceptance; v2 states release and supplies two repository addresses, whose availability cannot be verified from the PDFs. v2 also adds Optimal Checklists implementation details, token usage and an estimated USD 1.12 per fold, CPU feasibility discussion, and more explicit data-flow pseudocode. The previously specified decision-tree minimum leaf size is omitted.

R1.justification: v2 newly recognizes Zhang et al.'s Optimal Checklists as an existing unit-weighted checklist learner and revises the central comparison toward fixed-feature selection versus automatic derived-rule construction throughout the introduction, related work, and Tables 2/7. Appendix C.2 also adds positioning relative to FunSearch, OPRO, and LLM-SR. This substantially revises research positioning beyond bibliographic edits.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled 'Automatic Construction of Clinical Scoring Systems with LLM Agents'. Contributions, related work, method explanations, baseline discussion, and conclusion receive focused rewrites; acknowledgments and appendix subsections are added. The overall section sequence and much of the existing narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is enlarged across both columns and its caption expanded; all eight figures retain their artwork. v2 adds a main-text algorithm summary and Appendix Tables 11, 13, and 14, extends several comparison tables, and relocates four PLR rows. The overall visual style remains stable.

improvement.justification: The direct Optimal Checklists comparison and shared-rule-pool controls address important gaps in v1's prior-work comparison and attribution of performance gains. Together with corrected research positioning, these substantially strengthen the paper's scientific case. Privacy and missingness audits add useful bounded evidence. Conflicting hyperparameter/split descriptions and unexplained differences between external-validation result sets still limit reproducibility, but the central comparison and attribution gains are substantial.
